lead.text: scan_url(url) is a call-graph-root (EntryPoint) whose `url` parameter is fully attacker-controlled and flows unsanitized into _http_get(url): urllib.parse.urlparse(url) feeds parsed_url.netloc directly into http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc) and parsed_url.path/query directly into conn.request("GET", path_and_query), with no host/scheme allowlist. On a 302 response, _http_get recursively calls itself with response.headers["Location"] (attacker/server-controlled) with no depth limit and no re-validation, so a malicious/compromised server can redirect the scanner to arbitrary internal hosts. This is a Server-Side Request Forgery sink: any caller that passes user-supplied input into scan_url (e.g. a web service letting users submit a model URL to scan) lets the attacker make the scanning host issue HTTPS connections to arbitrary network destinations, chained through unlimited redirects.

lead.text: scan_huggingface_model(repo_id) is an EntryPoint whose `repo_id` parameter is attacker-controlled and is interpolated unsanitized into a URL string passed to _http_get: f"https://huggingface.co/api/models/{repo_id}" (and, on the resolve path, a similarly built download URL). The destination host is fixed, so this is a narrower variant of the scan_url SSRF (request/parameter injection against a pinned host) rather than full SSRF, but it is the same unsanitized-input-to-outbound-request pattern.

lead.text: In RelaxedZipFile.open() (src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py), after constructing the ZipExtFile for a 'r'-mode read, the code explicitly disables zip entry integrity validation with the comment 'Disable CRC validation as PyTorch may not use it' via `zef._expected_crc = None`. This removes the CRC32 integrity check that zipfile.ZipExtFile would normally enforce when reading an archive member to completion, meaning a corrupted or deliberately tampered zip entry (e.g. a crafted .pt/.bin/.zip model file submitted to scan_file_path/scan_url/scan_huggingface_model/scan_zip_bytes) will be read and handed to the pickle opcode scanner without any detection of truncation or tampering that CRC checking would normally catch. reason: The code exists exactly as described (confirmed by reading source), but the security framing is inverted: disabling CRC validation here does NOT create a scanner bypass — leaving CRC validation ENABLED would be the actual bypass vector, and the disabling is what prevents it. In cpython's zipfile.ZipExtFile, `_update_crc` (zipfile/__init__.py:1107-1115) raises `BadZipFile` the instant `self._eof` becomes True and the running CRC mismatches the expected one. Critically, `_eof` is set True as soon as the entry's full declared size has been produced by a single internal `_read1()` call (zipfile/__init__.py:1183-1186), regardless of how many bytes the caller actually asked for — and `_read1` always decompresses at least `MIN_READ_SIZE` (4096) bytes per call. Pickle metadata entries inside .pt/.bin archives are typically well under 4KB, so the very first read (picklescan's own magic-byte peek, `scanner.py:450` `magic_bytes = file.read(8)`) fully decompresses the entry and triggers the CRC check immediately — BEFORE `scan_pickle_bytes` is ever invoked. If CRC validation were left enabled, an attacker who simply corrupts a malicious pickle entry's recorded CRC32 would cause `BadZipFile` to be raised at that first read; `scan_zip_bytes`'s own `except (zipfile.BadZipFile, RuntimeError)` handler (`scanner.py:462-464`) catches this, logs only a warning, and skips the file entirely — so the dangerous pickle opcodes inside would NEVER reach the scanner. That is exactly the scenario `tests/init_data_files.py:initialize_corrupt_zip_file_crc` / `tests/test_scanner.py:385` (`malicious1_crc.zip` → still detects `Global('builtins','eval',Dangerous)`) is built to guard against, and it only passes because CRC checking IS disabled. So the disabling is a tested anti-evasion/compatibility measure, not a weakened integrity control that lets malicious content slip past undetected — the actual pickle-opcode scan (the tool's real security boundary) still runs on whatever bytes are present either way; CRC32 is a non-cryptographic checksum that offers no tamper-resistance against a motivated attacker in the first place. There is no demonstrated path by which this code change lets a dangerous payload bypass detection; the cited test demonstrates the opposite outcome.
evidence: src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py:88-93 (zef._expected_crc = None) exists as claimed; call path scanner.py:444 scan_zip_bytes -> RelaxedZipFile(data,"r"), confirmed reachable via EntryPoint query (method_full_name='src/picklescan/scanner.py:<module>.scan_zip_bytes', exposure='reachable', kind='handler'). scanner.py:448-464 shows the try/except that swallows zipfile.BadZipFile/RuntimeError per-entry, discarding any findings collected by that call. Stdlib zipfile (/usr/lib/python3.14/zipfile/__init__.py:1107-1115, 1169-1188) shows _update_crc raises BadZipFile as soon as _eof is set, and _eof is set once the full declared entry size is produced by a single _read1 call (which always reads >=4096 bytes), meaning a small CRC-mismatched pickle entry would raise on the very first read (scanner.py:450) if CRC checking were active. tests/init_data_files.py:453-731 (initialize_corrupt_zip_file_crc writing malicious1_crc.zip) and tests/test_scanner.py:385 (assert_scan("malicious1_crc.zip", [Global("builtins","eval",Dangerous)])) confirm the dangerous global IS detected in a CRC-mismatched zip — proving the disabled check does not cause missed detections, and would in fact be the mechanism of a missed detection if re-enabled.
